blogs.title: Neither Type 1 Nor Type 2: When to Suspect MODY in Young-Onset Diabetes
blogs.description: This post explores the persistent diagnostic challenge of distinguishing Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) from conventional Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes. Using the case as a springboard, it reviews the overlapping clinical features—such as young age at onset, symptomatic hyperglycemia with weight loss, and variable BMI—that make MODY easy to miss. The post outlines a practical clinical approach: when to suspect MODY based on family history patterns (autosomal dominant transmission across generations), the absence of islet autoantibodies (GADA, IA-2A, ZnT8), preserved C-peptide levels, and the lack of insulin resistance features like acanthosis nigricans. It also addresses the growing challenge of distinguishing MODY from T2DM as obesity rises globally, making BMI and metabolic syndrome less reliable discriminators than previously thought. The discussion emphasizes that MODY accounts for 1–6% of young-onset diabetes and is almost certainly underdiagnosed, with significant implications for treatment and family counseling.

blogs.title: When the Database Comes Up Empty: Making Sense of Novel Genetic Variants in MODY
blogs.description: This post dives into the practical challenge of interpreting a novel HNF1A variant (p.N270S) that was absent from ClinVar, VarSome, and published literature at the time of identification. It walks through the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) framework for variant classification, illustrating how multiple independent lines of evidence—adjacency to known pathogenic residues, a high AlphaMissense score (0.995), and family segregation with diabetes—were combined to classify this variant as likely pathogenic. The post discusses the critical role of next-generation sequencing (NGS) panels in expanding the known mutational spectrum of MODY genes, the distinction between a variant's novelty and its clinical relevance, and why absence from databases should not be equated with benign status. It also touches on the broader issue of how databases like ClinVar are biased toward well-studied populations, and how clinicians and geneticists in underrepresented populations must rely on functional prediction tools and segregation data when databases fall short.

blogs.title: From Insulin to GLP-1: Precision Therapeutics in HNF1A-MODY
blogs.description: This post examines how a confirmed genetic diagnosis of HNF1A-MODY directly transformed this patient's treatment trajectory—from an initial empiric regimen of basal insulin plus metformin and a DPP-4 inhibitor, to discontinuation of insulin and transition to a GLP-1 receptor agonist (dulaglutide), and finally to a simplified metformin plus DPP-4 inhibitor maintenance regimen. It reviews the evidence base for different therapeutic strategies in HNF1A-MODY: low-dose sulfonylureas as traditional first-line agents, emerging data supporting GLP-1 receptor agonists as a safer and equally effective alternative (particularly with lower hypoglycemia risk), and the rationale for metformin as adjunctive therapy. The post discusses the clinical decision-making process of weighing residual beta-cell function (assessed via stimulated C-peptide), treatment burden, and hypoglycemia risk when individualizing therapy. It frames this as a concrete example of precision medicine in action—where molecular diagnosis directly informs pharmacologic choice, reduces unnecessary treatment burden, and potentially preserves endogenous insulin secretion.

blogs.title: The SGLT-2 Trap: Why a Popular Drug Class May Be Dangerous in HNF1A-MODY
blogs.description: This post focuses on a specific and clinically urgent pharmacologic nuance: the heightened risk of SGLT-2 inhibitors in patients with HNF1A-MODY. It explains the molecular mechanism by which HNF1A mutations reduce transcription of the SGLT2 gene in renal tubules, lowering the renal threshold for glucose reabsorption and causing glycosuria independent of plasma glucose levels. This baseline reduction in SGLT2 activity means that pharmacologic SGLT2 inhibition in these patients can lead to excessive glucosuria, severe dehydration, and even euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis—risks that may outweigh any glycemic benefit. The post discusses how this drug-gene interaction represents a paradigm for precision pharmacotherapy: a medication class that is broadly beneficial in T2DM but potentially harmful in a specific monogenic diabetes subtype. It also reviews a published report of HNF1A-MODY patients developing severe dehydration and DKA due to SGLT2 inhibition, and provides practical guidance on avoiding this drug class until MODY has been genetically excluded in young-onset diabetes patients.

blogs.title: C-Peptide and the Glucagon Stimulation Test: Reclaiming a Forgotten Diagnostic Tool in Diabetes Subtyping
blogs.description: This post takes a deep dive into the utility of C-peptide measurement and the glucagon stimulation test (GST) in differentiating MODY from Type 1 diabetes. Using this patient's stimulated C-peptide of 0.83 nmol/L (above the 0.60 nmol/L cutoff for preserved beta-cell function) as a focal point, it reviews the physiology of C-peptide as a marker of endogenous insulin secretion, the practical aspects of performing the GST, and its role as a supportive (not definitive) diagnostic tool. The post discusses the nuances of interpreting C-peptide values: how preserved fasting C-peptide >0.6 ng/mL argues against Type 1 diabetes but how early Type 1 diabetes can also show normal values initially, necessitating longitudinal monitoring. It also covers how C-peptide data complement autoantibody testing and clinical features in building a case for MODY genetic testing, and how stimulated C-peptide can guide treatment decisions (e.g., whether insulin can be safely discontinued in favor of oral or injectable non-insulin therapies). The post positions C-peptide assessment as an underutilized but high-yield tool in the evaluation of ambiguous young-onset diabetes.

blogs.title: The Exeter MODY Calculator: A Useful Tool With a Population Problem
blogs.description: This post critically examines the MODY probability calculator developed by the Exeter group—a widely used clinical decision aid that estimates the likelihood of MODY based on clinical parameters—and its limitations when applied to non-White European populations. Using this case (where the calculator estimated a 62.4% MODY probability) as a launching point, the discussion covers how the tool was derived and validated primarily in White European cohorts and may overestimate MODY probability in other ethnic groups, potentially leading to unnecessary genetic testing or misallocation of resources. The post explores broader themes of population bias in clinical prediction tools, the challenge of applying algorithms developed in one population to genetically and phenotypically diverse groups, and the importance of population-specific prevalence data for MODY (citing studies in Chinese, Russian, and Danish populations). It argues for the development and validation of population-calibrated prediction models and for clinician awareness of the limitations of existing tools when practicing in diverse settings, while acknowledging that the calculator remains a valuable starting point for clinical decision-making.
